text: The Operating Systems course felt like it started with good intentions but never quite righted itself once the term got going. I have a strong coding background, but the theory side always lagged behind, and the early lectures left me more tangled than clarified—especially that first week when we debated process scheduling as if it were a math puzzle and not something I’d actually apply. The delivery relies heavily on recorded lectures, which are useful for catching details, but they’re dry and hard to stay engaged with after a long day juggling multiple demanding courses; I end up pausing and rewinding more than once just to keep the thread. Most of the time I worked solo, with little peer interaction or collaboration structure to lean on, so when I hit a snag that required discussion, I felt stuck and frustrated because feedback arrived too late to help, often missing the crucial midterm window. The prerequisite gaps I expected to be filled by this course were better addressed than I anticipated, but the overall organization felt scattershot, like deadlines moved predictably enough to miss the real rocks, and the term’s chaos reflected in my barely-passed grade. One memorable moment was an early confusion around virtual memory that colored the rest of the term, shaping how I approached every later topic. In comparing it to another course from the same term, this one left me more drained, even though I appreciated the practical concrete aspects of a small project we did late in the term.

I came in with real curiosity, but Data Structures with Dr. Park felt rough midsemester: the tool setup ate hours and grading seemed mismatched with lectures, yet I appreciated his clear explanations, even as the dry recorded lectures wore on.

I took Machine Learning more because the schedule fit my week than because I was hype about theory, and that showed in how I approached it. The recorded lectures are useful when I’m juggling a heavy midsemester grind, though they feel a bit dry and tend to repeat the same points, which I guess is fine when you’re catching up late. The software stack started rough for me—lots of environment hiccups and version mismatches—but it smooths out after a few tweaks, which is tolerable. I remember one office hours session where I finally got a straight answer on a data split quirk, which felt like a rescue; without that, I’d have flailed longer. Grading comments come after the fact and are detailed but delayed, so I’m left guessing a bit until feedback shows up.

The OS course became the main focus this term and I ended up chasing deadlines, falling behind, then catching up just before the week’s end. Grading felt transparent enough, though feedback came fast with thin explanations, and the setup tools were more frustrating than helpful for me.

I slogged through Operating Systems my last term, mostly because I focused on it as my main course, but the prereqs felt heavier than advertised and the steps felt slow to get feedback. The grading comments come in late yet are detailed, and group study helps more than solo puzzling.

Database Systems with Prof. Cohen felt like it clicked only when I already knew the adjacent material, and the advanced vibe didn’t save me from the stress of flaky tooling that ruined a couple of deadlines. The slides are serviceable but not memorable, and yes, the email support is slow when deadlines hit, so I ended up figuring most things out myself. I did learn a few concrete ideas in office hours, though—still not sure the C I earned reflects understanding.

Database Systems with Prof. Haddad was a mixed ride in the middle of a brutal semester for me: I leaned on a study group to keep up because the platform quirks kept tripping me up and the lectures felt distant, so the pace and explanations didn’t always click. The assignments varied a lot in how feedback came back, and the exam format surprised me with a few tricky SQL design questions that weren’t hammered in class. Overall I learned a lot, but I didn’t love the experience.

I’m in the first semester and I treated Machine Learning as my main focus that term, mostly relying on recordings and notes because live lectures clashed with a lot of labs. Prof. Rios is clear enough when she’s actually online, and the prerequisite material helped fill gaps better than I expected, but the tooling hiccups near deadlines made weeks feel messier than they should have been. Group work adds value when our team functions well, though I’ll admit I dreaded some pushbacks in the beginning. The exams and project feel like they’re aligned with the assignments, and I’d recommend broadly, especially if you’re juggling other courses; I remember one office-hours chat where she suggested a different approach for the final memo that clicked for me.

Cyber Security Basics was an advanced elective that felt doable only if you already know some adjacent material, and the curve after the first few weeks was… tricky. I was trying to fit short evening sessions around a stack of deadlines that suddenly piled up, and the feedback came quickly enough to adjust in theory but often arrived too late to salvage the current week’s work; still, the quick notes helped for the next assignment. I’d still say I’d recommend broadly, but not without a shrug and a few groans about

Taking Machine Learning with Prof. Alvarez felt doable even though I was juggling a couple of other tough courses. The workload tilted positive for me because the project-heavy vibe kept me engaged, and I actually looked forward to tweaking the model right up to the high-stakes exams week. Feedback comes quickly enough to adjust, but sometimes it lands after a deadline that’s already moved, which was a hiccup I didn’t love. TAs were responsive and practical, especially when I got stuck on feature scaling. The one memorable moment was that surprise long-form quiz during the midterm sprint—it stuck with me how notes from the week before helped more than I expected. Overall, I’d still recommend it if you want to build real hands-on intuition.

Taking Computer Networks with Prof. Alvarez in my first semester while working full-time, I fell behind around deadlines but managed to catch up; the project-heavy setup and high-stakes exams felt useful but not enjoyable, and the weekly pace varied oddly.

Calculus II with Prof. Haddad started accessible but ramps up fast, and the workload felt brutal for my coding-heavy, weak theory background; the tool setup wasted hours for marginal payoff, though lectures were clear, and peer discussions saved me at times—I'll still barely passed after a rough term.

I picked Computer Networks mainly to fit my term, and while Dr. Chen’s slides were serviceable and not especially memorable, the course only clicked for me after a late-semester push and a study group; deadlines dragged, email support was slow, and the grading rubric felt vague.

Data Structures felt a bit too fast for my first-semester brain, and the prerequisites assumed more math and code basics than I’d expected; I started off engaged but attendance faded as midsemester crunch hit, especially with the quirky deadline bursts and a heavy project that didn’t map neatly to lectures with Prof. Alvarez.

Linear Algebra was solid enough for where I am in the term, and I’ll admit my stronger coding background helped me keep up, especially since I treated it as my main focus course. The lectures were clear and paced reasonably, but the assessment setup felt unforgiving: few tests, yet each one mattered a lot, which kept me grinding for the grade band I landed—a solid B that matched the effort I poured in. The grading rubric, though, still feels vague in spots, so I spent more time second-guessing what the graders wanted than I’d like. One concrete thing that sticks is the single big project near midterm that tied everything together, and I wish there had been a little more peer discussion; mostly it was individual work, which is fine, just not very motivating for me.

Linear Algebra in my last semester was frustratingly inaccessible at times, especially as the course ramped up from the early slides into heavier proofs without enough concrete grounding. TAs answered promptly and gave practical tips, but instructions left too much room for interpretation, so I spent extra hours decoding expectations. One memorable week was the midterm where the format felt fluid and I couldn’t rely on a single model solution, plus the project deadline pattern was a real grind. Overall, I wouldn’t recommend despite some value.

Midway through this heavy semester, Database Systems has felt like a tough ramp-up for someone new to the discipline. I came in with the basics from the prerequisites, and the lectures are clear enough, with pacing that doesn’t sprint past you, which I appreciate while juggling a full-time job. The LMS flows smoothly and I can usually submit without scrambling, but the feedback arrives in fits and starts, which makes it feel like I’m racing a deadline on my own time. I compared it to the easier prerequisite and it’s a different animal—the project felt doable in principle but the timing and the sparse comments left me unsure how to adjust. Still, the instructor lays out concepts that stick when I’m not overwhelmed, and I’m sort of hopeful I’ll land something solid by the end.

Started the semester pretty engaged, stayed that way for the first few weeks, and then the energy dip hit as I started juggling full-time work again. The lectures were clear and paced fine, and I actually liked how the group projects sometimes clicked when everyone pulled their weight, plus it was nice to hear peers explain things in a way that finally clicked for me. I built on the prerequisites without too much trouble, but the course leaned heavily on reports and time management, which felt rough when I had to fit them around late shifts. By mid-semester attendance faded a bit—not because of disinterest, more because life kept intruding and motivation wavered in fits, though I still finished with a sense of having learned something practical. The turning point for me was a late-semester group problem where we split tasks well and I realized I could see the threat model clearly, even if I wasn’t sure I could articulate every part in the final. If the team didn’t function well, the value dropped, and that stuck with me. Overall, it’s solid for the basics, albeit pretty report-heavy and time-consuming, and I’m left unsure whether I fully internalized all the concepts.

I took Machine Learning mainly out of curiosity, and the lectures were solid enough even though the pace ramps up quickly. I mostly relied on recordings and notes because evenings after a heavy class day aren’t great for live questions, and office hours saved me once I hit a wall on feature scaling. The grading comments helped after a delay, and I remember one early confusion about bias-variance that kind of stuck with me as the term wore on.

Took Database Systems with Prof. Alvarez while working full-time, and the pace got rough mid-semester; the concepts clicked, but the examples felt thin and the group work guidelines were unclear. Quick feedback helped adjust, but I wouldn’t take it again despite some value.

I stuck with Database Systems mainly because the schedule fit better than my interests, and I did end up needing to catch up around deadlines after falling behind. Prof. Haddad’s recorded lectures helped a bit, though they’re pretty dry; the real friction was the tooling setup and quirks of the platform, which made the whole process feel unnecessarily stressful. The exams felt fair enough, but the load and pacing were exhausting, and I finally landed in an A after a curve, which felt more about timing than clarity.

i took machine learning with dr. chen and felt kind of stuck between proofs comfort and the messy real system stuff we never fully covered. the week-by-week pace felt uneven, and the platform quirks plus sloppy communication added stress right when a deadline loomed; i remember a midterm where the questions wandered into tiny edge cases that felt more stress than insight. the grading curve helped me land an a, but the overall vibe left me wondering if the material clicked outside of adjacent topics.

I signed up for Linear Algebra thinking it would be a quick boost, and the workload ended up being oddly doable for an advanced elective—lots of project work and a couple of high-stakes exams that kept me on my toes. Dr. Park kept up with nearly every lecture, and I almost never fell behind, but the feedback arrived fast while explanations felt thinner, so I had to piece things together myself. The forums helped when they weren’t a bit dismissive, and I’d only recommend this course with serious

I took Database Systems in my last semester because it fit my schedule more than my interests, and as a returning student I felt rusty but the basics came back enough to keep up. The platform and submission flow were smooth, but the examples felt thin and the move from accessible prerequisites to sharp ramp-up was jarring. I remember one late-night assignment that hinged on a tricky query plan, and it didn’t help that collaboration expectations were unclear.

Data Structures with Prof. Alvarez was rough at first—the tooling setup and the report-heavy pace hung over me as a full-time worker, but the later lectures and office-hour tips started to click, especially around the forum threads and a late TA session that helped me barely pass.

Calculus II with Dr. Singh felt like a mid-program gauntlet that started accessible but ramps up sharply, especially once you’re staring at those integrals with trigonometric substitutions and partial fractions around week six. I mostly relied on recordings and notes, since live lectures drifted into quick recaps and the occasional chalk-demo that didn’t always click, and the calendar deadlines didn’t help my focus either. The group work had its moments when the team functioned well—one partner kept bringing in a clean, worked example and it saved me on the next quiz—but other times it devolved into everyone chasing their own approach and the shared solution ended up messy. Tooling was a pain: the online problem set interface is clunky, and the grader’s hints felt oddly cryptic, which you notice most when you’re under time pressure during a Friday rush. The grading mix doesn’t quite line up with what the lectures emphasize, which left me juggling expectations and eventually relying on the notes more than the lectures themselves. Honestly, I would not take it again, even though I did finish with a better grasp of integrals, and I remember the project’s hint about a clever substitution more than anything else.

Taking Linear Algebra with Prof. Haddad in my last semester before graduation felt like a gamble between schedule fit and actually learning something useful. The slides were serviceable but not memorable, so I ended up skimming them and using the textbooks more than I’d care to admit, especially since the pacing and feedback timing varied a lot by assignment. I appreciated the human side of the lecturer, but the grading felt uneven—high-stakes exams paired with a heavy project load made the whole thing stressful, and the policies were fine in theory, but communication around deadlines often felt sloppy. The one week that sticks is the eigenvalue week where one tricky breeze of a problem set showed up, and I finally clicked something—that small win sticks, even as I question the overall approach. I’m not sure whether I’d recommend it, given the mixed experience and the sense I’d earned my way through it more than benefited from it.

I took Data Structures mainly because I needed it for the specialization, and I’m still glad I did it, even though the ride was messier than I expected. The workload felt heavy but in a way that pushed me to actually plan ahead, and the few big assessments each mattered a lot, so you don’t drift through the term. The tooling was solid enough to get through the labs, which helped since I’m comfortable with proofs but not so much with systems-y stuff, and that contrast kept the class feeling like a test of foundations rather than a coding slog. I came in comparing it to the easier prerequisite, and yes, it’s stricter about rigor, but the practical payoff wasn’t as immediate as I’d hoped; still, the projects showed how the concepts stick in real problems. What really stuck was how the collaboration window felt fuzzy—unclear what to expect from group work—and the administration could be fine in policy but sloppy in communication, like a note that never quite reaches you. Feedback came sparse and late, which stung when an early misstep would have saved me, and deadlines piled up in a way that made the week feel like a sprint I hadn’t trained for. One small incident, the last-minute tool update before the final, stands out as the moment everything clicked and then crashed again in a way that only makes sense in hindsight.

The Cyber Security Basics course got me curious from week one, and I stuck with it because the tooling finally clicked after a bit of setup, which felt worth it once I started coding along. I’d say the one memorable moment was the week we tackled a practical exam; it forced me to apply what I’d learned rather than just memorize. Feedback varied, but TAs were responsive and useful when I reached out.

Took Database Systems while juggling a full-time job, and it was a roller. The software stack is rough at first but you can wrestle through it after a few late nights; I ended up catching up around the deadlines but it wasn’t pretty getting there. The reporting-heavy work ate up real hours and I felt the grading matched the effort, mostly solid B territory, which was fair but not comforting. Instructions left a lot to interpretation, and feedback was sparse until it was already too late to change much. I remember my TA in office hours shakily wiring up a quick data-model example and saying to just push through the messy setup—totally stayed with me, oddly practical but not enjoyable.

Starting with a general verdict, I’d say Calculus II was useful in moments but not enjoyable, especially as the middle of a brutal semester wore me down. The workload felt heavy, and the exam fairness left me feeling off, like the questions sometimes relied on tricky edge cases rather than clear understanding. I came in relatively engaged in week one, but attendance faded as the pace intensified and the time I’d hoped to dedicate to this plus a couple other demanding courses evaporated. The course did build on the prerequisites, and I could see how the ideas linked to what we learned before, which helped when I did have quiet hours to actually sit with the material. The LMS was smooth enough for submissions, but the feedback usually arrived late or sparsely, so I’d stumble into the next set of problems half-lit. A concrete memory stands out: during the big midterm, the format shifted to more problem sets under a tight clock, and there was a small grading quirk on partial credit that felt unfair. Overall I feel mixed: it was a tool I could use, but the fatigue and the timing around feedback made it hard to enjoy.

Calculus II was a required drag in my advanced elective lineup, and I mainly stuck with it because of the grade hurdle more than any reading spark. I fell behind and only caught up around deadlines, and the grading rubric never felt clear to me, which made the few quizzes feel like a moving target; the forums could be helpful yet occasionally dismissive, especially when questions weren’t “officially” answered. I liked the instructor, but the mismatch between what was taught and the assessment left me with mixed feelings,

Taking Calculus II in the middle of a heavy semester was rough for me as a returning student who felt rusty, and I did notice my attendance fade a bit after the initial weeks with Prof. Haddad. Lectures were clear and paced decently, but the jump from the earlier topics to the harder integration techniques ramps up fast, and the prerequisite fit starts accessible before it suddenly tightens. I relied on the forums a lot; they helped, though sometimes the dismissive replies left me wondering if I was asking the wrong thing. Tooling issues during a couple deadlines didn’t help either, and by week eight I was juggling a mid-semester crunch that didn’t make the course any more enjoyable, but I still think it’s broadly worth sticking with.

Taking Data Structures in my first semester mostly matched my curiosity, and the pacing felt doable even though motivation came in fits and starts. Prof. Alvarez delivers clear, bite-sized explanations and the LMS submission flow is smooth, but feedback arrives late enough to be almost useless for the next assignment, and some graded items felt off with what was taught in lectures. A small project on a linked list felt memorable, mixed with how the exam format lingered in the back of my mind.

Summer term with compressed pacing, I mostly did things solo and felt the grading rubric was vague; the project-heavy load and high-stakes exams pushed me, and while it helped my proofs, it didn’t feel fair or transparent, especially Dr. Park’s office hours.

Midway through the semester I signed up for Data Structures mostly because the evening slots fit my schedule, not because I was crazy about graphs and trees. The software stack started rough—some tool kept crashing during the coding labs, and I felt the setup ate into the first couple of weeks—but it gets manageable after you push through. The course leaned heavy on a few big projects and high-stakes exams, and I fell behind when another hard class piled on, then barely caught up as deadlines loomed; the feedback came fast but often felt thin, like a quick score with little explanation. I’m not sure I’d recommend it, even though a couple of concrete assignments stood out, and there’s a turning point later where I finally saw how the pieces fit, but the overall grind is exhausting.

I’m in the middle of a heavy semester, and Cyber Security Basics by Prof. Rios has been a mixed bag that somehow kept me going. The slides are serviceable but not memorable, and the workload feels doable but the few assessments carry a lot of weight, which makes me anxious about how my understanding lines up with the grade I might get. I fell behind around midterms and only caught up as deadlines loomed, though I did appreciate that there was some late feedback when I emailed, even if that support came slowly during crunch times. I remember popping into office hours once and bouncing a concrete question about a phishing scenario, which helped a bit, but I’m still unsure if a C reflects my grasp or just the grading quirk.

Cyber Security Basics was a decent fit for me since I’m new to the field and juggling this last semester with a full-time job. The workload felt doable but kept me on my toes, especially with a few high-stakes assessments where a single mistake could derail a grade, though the grading comments came a bit late to act on. Dr. Chen’s instruction sometimes seemed uneven week to week, and the instructions left a bit too much room for interpretation, which added unnecessary friction at times. I appreciated the detailed feedback once it finally appeared, and the course overall kept me moving toward the track’s requirements, but I still felt exhausted by how demanding it could be, even as I managed. One concrete moment I’ll remember: the capstone-like lab where we had to configure a basic firewall rule set under a looming deadline.

I took Computer Networks with Prof. Cohen while juggling a full-time job, so I mostly relied on recordings and notes, which helped but sometimes felt behind the pace of the live class. The workload was heavy and quite deadline-driven, with frequent assignments that stressed timing more than deep understanding, though the prerequisite buildup did help me feel less lost. The forums were useful yet a bit dismissive at times, and one memorable week near the midterm sticks in my mind because the exam format changed last minute and that scramble was rough.

Computer Networks was an intro service course I took because it’s required, and Dr. Chen kept us afloat with office hours that rescued the weeklies. The material felt neutral, and the pace was uneven, but the assignment-heavy schedule kept me moving, barely passing.

I stuck with nearly every lecture for Calculus II, and Prof. Rios generally kept the pace steady, though the explanations sometimes felt thin while deadlines cropped up fast. With a strong coding background but weaker theory, I found the assessment mix a bit off, and the grading rubric vague, which didn’t help my study plan. The forums helped, but a few posts came off as dismissive; I remember one office-hours visit where we talked through a tricky integration method and the tutor teased me for overthinking it, which stuck with me. Overall I’d still recommend it broadly, just go in ready for quick

I took Linear Algebra mid-semester, mostly because I heard it would be useful for industry work, and I’ll admit Dr. Park makes the concepts click better than I expected. The explanations are solid, but the examples feel a bit thin at times, which didn’t help during the rough mid-semester crunch when I was juggling a lot. The few assessments are meaningful and you can’t coast—one big project stood out as a real grinder, but it’s your chance to actually show you know the material. It helps to have a study group; the class just makes more sense when you bounce ideas around. The LMS flow is smooth, and I compared it to my easier prerequisite and realized this one actually makes you think about how the ideas connect.

I took Linear Algebra as my main focus that term, juggling it with a full-time job and a schedule that fit nothing else nicely, and I ended up with a messed mix of feelings. The instructor clearly nails the conceptual stuff—the explanations click when we talk about vectors and linear transformations, but the examples felt thin and I kept wondering, “how does this apply to my problem set or that project?” The tooling setup was a constant headache at first, which made the early weeks feel unnecessarily frustrating, and I wish the software stack had been smoother from day one. Still, the course does work better if you form a study group; I leaned on peers to fill in the gaps, and that helped when the graded parts started to pile up. I liked the instructor, but the grading pattern rubbed me the wrong way, especially since I was trying to juggle work and deadlines, which didn’t help my motivation. By the end I was barely passing and felt mixed about the whole thing, yet a few concepts finally settled and I could see where the math might show up again.

Machine Learning felt like a required hurdle in the middle of a brutal semester, and I mostly kept up by balancing it with two other heavy courses. The setup for tools took more effort than the payoff, and the collaboration expectations were unclear, but it helped that I already knew some adjacent material, so it didn’t derail me. A memory anchor is the first week confusion that shuffled my approach for the rest of term. I’d still recommend it broadly.

Calculus II started accessible enough with the first weeks, but the pace ramps up sharply and left me juggling more abstract theory than I’m used to from a coding-heavy background. I stayed on top of nearly every lecture, but the instructions often felt vague, leaving a lot of room for interpretation and a sense that the grading comments wouldn’t show up until far after each deadline. The few assessments mattered a lot, and a late turning point in week eight still sticks with me—the test format felt suddenly stiff, and I left with mixed feelings even though I managed to pass. The feedback when it did arrive was detailed, but the delay undercut its usefulness, and I can’t shake the sense that the course organization didn’t quite hold up under the workload.

The OS course felt useful enough to justify the time, but I won’t pretend I enjoyed it. The lectures were clear and the pacing was fine, which helped since I’m comfortable with proofs but not so much with actual systems work; still, the workload landed as a handful, with a few chapters worth of concepts and one big project that mattered more than the weekly quizzes. Most of the work was solo, and while I didn’t rely much on peers, I did notice the help from classmates more than from staff when I hit a snag. A concrete gripe: the grading felt skewed toward one final assessment, so small mistakes could sting, even though the topics themselves are solidly grounded. Overall, it’s a usable course, but I left frustrated yet fair about its usefulness.

I signed up for Cyber Security Basics more because it fit my schedule than because I was obsessed with the topic, and that showed in my pacing—I fell behind and only caught up around deadlines. The instructor can explain concepts clearly, but the examples felt thin, like we were told what a threat is without seeing how it actually plays out in a real network; the forums helped, but sometimes the replies sounded a bit dismissive, which didn’t help when I was stuck. Group work sometimes adds value when the team clicks, but other times it dragged because someone wasn’t pulling their weight. My grade ended up in the C range, and I’m not sure it truly reflected my grasp of the material, especially since the assessment mix didn’t line up with the lectures I watched. For a concrete memory, I’ll note the weekly lab required a quick pivot on the same topic, which felt fair but also exposed how thin the examples were. If I compare it to another

I took Cyber Security Basics as a mid-program core course and ended up making it my main focus this term, since it was a prerequisite for the specialization I’m chasing. The lectures and slides were serviceable but not memorable, and I found myself leaning on the peer discussion chats and our TAs more than the official materials when I hit a snag. The collaboration structure helped a lot—talking through tricky week 4 concepts in a small group kept me from spiraling on the readings, even when the instructions felt a bit vague and left too much room for interpretation. My grade landed in a solid B, which felt fair for the effort I put in, though I did notice the grading seemed to hinge on a few ambiguous rubric items rather than clear milestones. I’d only recommend taking it with solid prep and a good plan to use office hours or forums, since relying on email support during deadline crunches was slow. One memorable moment was the week of the capstone-style assignment, where a tight deadline pushed me to actually draft questions in the forums and compare notes with a classmate before submitting. Overall, I’d say it’s worth it if you’re prepared to lean on the community and tolerate the less-than-smooth admin cues.

Dr. Miller’s Linear Algebra kept me on my toes—pacing felt solid and the lecture cadence helped me haul through the tougher theory gaps, even with my coding-heavy background. TAs were practical and the project-heavy setup but grading comments were slow to arrive, which left me jittery after the big exams.

Summer term was rough juggling a full-time job and this mid-program core course; the pacing plus decompressed sessions felt slow, but the insistence on deep concepts helped, even though the platform quirks and slow email support stressed me during deadlines.

took Computer Networks as an intro service course while working full‑time, relied mostly on recordings and notes, and barely passed after I kept wrestling with the labs. the group work helped when the team clicked, but the tool setup ate time for the payoff.

I stuck with nearly every lecture, and the math clicked a bit, but the tooling setup and constant deadline hiccups made weeks feel longer than they were. The project on convergence proofs dragged, and I’m still unsure if my C reflected understanding or the tedious workflow.

I’m comfortable with proofs but this advanced elective in Computer Networks ramped up faster than I expected, and some weeks I felt behind the math while chasing the hardware-side projects. Prof. Alvarez is clearly sharp and I appreciated how approachable he can be in office hours, especially when I ran into a confusing bit about link-state vs distance-vector during a forum thread—he answered, point by point, which helped me focus on the right questions. The TAs were practical and responsive, but the feedback on my midterm arrived too late to fix the core issues, and I’m not sure the grade reflected what I actually understood. Peer discussions often mattered more than the official materials, and a concrete deadline quirk—an unusually early project checkpoint—made the whole thing feel more pressured than it needed to be.

Calculus II with Prof. Alvarez was a mixed bag: clear explanations when he punched through a concept, but the lectures felt dry and quick, and I barely scraped by after struggling most of the term. The TAs were practical and quick to respond, and the assignments piled up with tight deadlines, which kept me honest even on inconsistent motivation. I’ll admit I didn’t plan to take this again, yet it did push me to wrestle with proofs more than I expected.

I took Calculus II mainly because it’s required for my degree, and I approached it with a coding mindset but not much theory intuition, so I relied on the lectures more than I’d hoped. The instructor explains concepts, not just procedures, which I appreciated, but the examples felt thin and I kept wanting a few more concrete demonstrations to connect the ideas to code-like thinking I’m used to. Deadlines stacked up in weeks where tooling hiccups dragged things out, so some deadlines felt harsher than the work itself, especially when the online platform hiccuped during submission windows. The grading comments are detailed, but they came after the fact, which made it hard to adjust midstream, and I found that mismatch between what was emphasized in lectures and what was assessed a bit frustrating. I compared this to the prerequisite, which felt like an easier ride, and I found myself wishing for a quicker feedback loop to know whether my approach to problems was on the right track. Still, I’ll admit I liked the instructor’s tone and overall direction, even as the grading cadence and the thin set of worked examples kept nagging at me.

Midway through this heavy semester, I’ve found Linear Algebra with Prof. Haddad solid but mismatched in spots. The lectures are clear and the pace is reasonable, and peers are pretty engaged in the problem sets, which helps since I’m comfortable with proofs but not big on the systems stuff. Setup for the tooling is annoying and eats time that would be better spent thinking about concepts, though the quick feedback when scores land helps more than you’d expect.

Summer term felt rushed: I fell behind, then caught up near deadlines, and the pacing was actually smoother than I feared. Prof. Cohen’s recorded lectures helped, LMS flow was chill, but explanations are thin; still, the sharp ramp and quick feedback bugged me.

The Database Systems course fit my summer schedule more than my curiosity, and I barely crossed the line after wrestling with the first few weeks; office hours saved me, and when the team clicked the project finally clicked too, even though some feedback came late.

Cyber Security Basics felt like it matched the effort I threw into it, even though I’m new to the discipline and starting from basics. The workload was real but doable, especially since I was juggling a few other demanding courses, and I appreciated that the time pressure was mostly manageable week to week. The lectures were recorded, which helped when I fell behind, but they were a bit dry—hard to stay energized listening to long expositions, so I relied on short notes to stay engaged. The platform quirks did add unnecessary stress at times, with a couple of timeouts and a quirky quiz interface that slowed me down more than it should have. Group work added real value when the team clicked, though I had a few sessions where we stalled waiting for one member to pull their weight. Stuff like graded quick demos and a midterm that felt more about explaining steps than testing real understanding stuck with me; I’m glad the project was concrete enough to see progress, even if the explanations behind the fast feedback were thin.
